messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 79
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Combat Pilot
- Trauma Type: Police violence
- Pcl5: 80

She is seventy-nine now, a widowed Latin American woman who still carries herself like a pilot even when she is only walking from the kitchen to the living room. Her back stays straight. She notices exits without meaning to. She still folds dish towels with the same precision she once used to check maps and instruments. For years she made a life in the air, flying in combat, trusting procedure, discipline, and the belief that if she stayed alert enough she could get herself and others home. What unsettles her is that the event that breaks her does not happen in the sky, in war, or in any cockpit. It happens on the ground, in her own city, in broad daylight, at an age when she thinks she has already survived enough.

It begins after her husband has died, when she is living alone and learning the routines of widowhood. One afternoon she is driving back from the pharmacy. At an intersection near her neighborhood, police cars swarm around a young man on the sidewalk. She slows, startled by the shouting. An officer bangs on her window and orders her to stop the car and get out. She does not understand at first. She asks what is happening, and before she can fully unbuckle her seatbelt, the door is yanked open. She is pulled by the arm with a force that shocks her. She remembers saying, in a clear trained voice, “I am cooperating.” The words do nothing. Her cheek hits the pavement. A knee presses into her back. She hears someone say she is resisting. The absurdity of it flashes through her mind even as terror takes over: a seventy-something widow in orthopedic shoes, pinned like an enemy combatant.

What stays with her most is not pain, though she has bruises for weeks. It is the total inversion of reality. In the military, threat had structure. There were enemies, commands, contingencies. Here there is only confusion and the sickening discovery that authority can become arbitrary in an instant. She remembers the smell of hot asphalt, the grit in her mouth, the metallic taste of fear. She remembers trying to slow her breathing the way she had taught younger pilots under fire, but her body will not obey. One officer rifles through her purse while another keeps shouting. Eventually they realize she is not the person they are looking for. No one apologizes. One of them tells her she is free to go, as if she has merely been delayed.

Afterward she tells almost no one. She says she fell. She avoids the intersection. At night she lies awake replaying the scene with an excruciating clarity that feels more vivid than the room around her. She hears the command voice in her ears and feels her chest tighten. Sometimes she startles awake convinced someone is standing over her bed. She begins leaving lights on in the house, then feels ashamed of herself for being frightened in her own home.

She had once been known for calm under pressure. Friends from her flying years remember her as exacting, fearless, impossible to rattle. Now a siren in the distance can undo an entire day. If a police cruiser appears in traffic behind her, her hands become slick on the steering wheel and she has to fight the urge to pull over and abandon the car. At the grocery store, if she hears raised voices, she freezes and scans for cover before she even realizes what she is doing. She hates that instinct, hates that her body makes decisions before her mind catches up. She tells herself she is being ridiculous, but the self-criticism only leaves her more exhausted.

Her world gets smaller. She stops driving except when absolutely necessary. She turns down invitations, especially if they involve downtown streets or crowds. Her daughter notices that she no longer sits near windows in restaurants and that she flinches when strangers come too close. When family members urge her to report what happened, she becomes irritable, then abruptly silent. Part of her wants justice; another part cannot bear the thought of uniforms, statements, being doubted. She has spent a lifetime enduring hardship with discipline, and now she is humiliated by how little control she feels over her own reactions.

She often compares this fear to combat and cannot make sense of it. In war she had training, mission, comrades, purpose. Here she feels stripped of all of that, left with raw vigilance and no place to direct it. Some mornings she wakes already tense, jaw aching from clenching through the night. She checks the locks repeatedly. She sits in her armchair and listens for engines, for footsteps, for anything out of place. The television stays off because footage of arrests, protests, even flashing lights can send her heart racing. She says she no longer feels fully in the present; part of her remains on that pavement, waiting for the next blow, still trying to understand how she could survive combat only to be broken open by the people she was taught to trust.
